Second, after the blinding, Odysseus tied the sheep together in groups of three and hid himself beneath the largest ram by clinging to its fleece [3][4]. When Polyphemus opened the cave door to let his flocks out to pasture, he felt the sheep as they passed but could not detect the men hidden beneath them [3][4]. Odysseus and his comrades thus escaped with the sheep to their ships [3][4].

Achilles died by an arrow shot by Paris, the Trojan prince, guided by the god Apollo [1][2]. According to Ovid, Apollo, angered at Achilles, revealed himself to Paris and directed the Trojan's arrow at Achilles, with the fatal shaft striking him down during battle [1]. However, some sources present variations: Apollodorus notes in one passage that Achilles was killed by Apollo [3], while in another passage he records that Achilles was killed by Alexander (another name for Paris) [4]. Additionally, Ovid describes in another account that Achilles was killed by Paris and Apollo with arrows or shafts [5].

Achilles had been forewarned of his fate. Apollodorus records that Thetis, his mother, forewarned him that he would die by Apollo's hand if he killed Tenes, which he did, thus fulfilling this prophecy [3]. Similarly, Homer's Iliad indicates that Thetis foretold he would perish beneath the wall of the Trojans by the swift missiles of Apollo [6], and the dying Hector foretold that Achilles would be slain by Paris and Phoebus Apollo at the Scaean gate [7]. Homer also notes more broadly that Achilles was fated to be slain in fight by a god and a mortal [8], and that he was foretold to die in battle, smitten by a spear cast or an arrow from the string [9].

Achilles withdrew from the fighting after his quarrel with Agamemnon because Agamemnon took his prize, Briseis.
